t.2.38.1: Then, seeing the king lying on his bed, sunk in grief, Kausalyā, afflicted by sorrow for her son, spoke to that lord of the earth.
t.2.38.3: Having banished Rāma, she, fortunate, her desire attained and at ease, will terrify me again, like a vicious snake in the house.
t.2.38.2: O tiger among men, with Rāghava gone, Kaikeyī, having sown her poison like a two-tongued serpent, will surely roam about freely like a she-serpent that has cast off its skin.
t.2.38.4: Would that Rāma might live in the city, dwelling at home even if he went about begging alms! One was free to grant the boon even to the point of making my son a slave.
t.2.38.6: Surely the hero, mighty-armed and bearing his bow, whose gait is like that of a lordly elephant, is now entering the forest with his wife and with Lakṣmaṇa.
t.2.38.5: Having cast Rāma down from the place that was rightly his, you have allotted a portion to Kaikeyī as one who keeps the sacred fires allots a share to the rākṣasas at the parvan rite.
t.2.38.7: But what will become of them in the forest, those who have never known sorrow, abandoned by you to dwell in the forest with Kaikeyī's consent?
t.2.38.9: Will that auspicious time ever come now, bringing an end to my grief, when I may see Rāghava here again, together with his wife and with his brother?
t.2.38.8: Those young ones, stripped of their jewels and banished at the very season when they should be enjoying life's rewards, how will they live, poor wretches, making their meals of fruits and roots?
t.2.38.10: When will Ayodhyā, the glorious, having heard that the two heroes have returned, become a city of joyful people, garlanded with banners raised high?
t.2.38.11: When will the city, seeing those two tigers among men returned again from the forest, rejoice in delight, like the ocean swelling at the full moon?
t.2.38.12: When will the mighty-armed hero enter the city of Ayodhyā, placing Sītā before him in the chariot, like a bull leading a young cow?
t.2.38.13: When will thousands of people shower with parched grain my two sons, the subduers of foes, as they enter along the royal highway?
t.2.38.14: When will the cheerful maidens, offering fruits to the twice-born, joyfully walk around the city in reverent circumambulation?
t.2.38.15: When will he, mature in wisdom and in years, radiant as an immortal and knowing what is right, come to me, frolicking like a three-year-old child?
t.2.38.16: Without doubt, O hero, I think that long ago, cruel woman that I was, I severed the udders of mothers while their calves were longing to drink.
t.2.38.17: Like a cow robbed by a lion, I, who love my child, have been forcibly made calfless by Kaikeyī, O tiger among men, like a cow with a young calf.
t.2.38.18: For I, who have but one son, cannot bear to live without that son, endowed with every virtue and skilled in all the śāstras.
t.2.38.19: For, not seeing my beloved son, mighty-armed and mighty in strength, I find in myself no power at all to go on living here.
t.2.38.20: For this fire, sprung from grief for my son, has risen up and sets me ablaze, just as the blessed sun of surpassing splendour scorches this earth with its rays in the hot season.
